title: TA9-07359
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Colombia claims refugee protection pursuant to Sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Allegations
The claimant alleged the following in support of his claim.

The claimant alleges that due to an incident in XXXX, Department of Tolima, Colombia at the end of XXXX 2009, when an injured member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), with others in his band, arrived at the house of his brother, where the claimant was, demanding medical assistance and did not get it, that he is sought by the FARC, because he is perceived as having a political opinion contrary to the FARC.

In this incident, the Guerilla demanded that the claimant's brother-in-law go to town to get a doctor, and that the claimant and sister remain at the house as guarantees. While the brother-in-law was gone, the claimant was in the kitchen, when more shots were heard, then quiet; the injured party left with the others who had accompanied him.
The brother-in-law returned, alone, as no one was willing to come.
Fearing the FARC's return, the claimant and his family quickly left the house, and went their separate ways.

Later while hiding in Bogota, the claimant learned that the FARC went to his sister's to inquire about him and his sister in-law, because the FARC claimed that the claimant and his family had made them "victims" in XXXX.

As a result the claimant believes that he is perceived as having a political opinion which is contrary to the interests of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) because he did not provide the medical assistance to the FARC that day. Determination

I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in Colombia. I find that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to Colombia would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. The determinative issue is credibility, subjective fear, and re-availment of the claimant.

In making the assessment in this claim the panel considered the claimant's oral and written testimony, counsel's submissions made orally, and all other documentary evidence entered at the hearing. Identity

I accept that the claimant is a citizen of Colombia due to the identification provided at the Port of Entry,2 which included his Colombian Passport and United States Permanent Residence Card. Credibility
Maldonado3 requires the panel to accept as truthful, testimony, unless there is good reason to doubt the veracity.
There were inconsistencies in the claimant's story such as: * Who he lived with.

The claimant stated in the narrative that he had lived in a small village "I went to live with my wife in the town of XXXX, Department of Tolima, where my brother has a small house he gave me to use in exchange for taking care of it. In the following years we found a degree of peace..."4 According to the narrative, he lived peacefully with his wife.

The claimant provided a letter5 certifying that the "XXXX XXXX family resided at the property". This letter does not say who the members of the family were, and if the claimant was one of them. As a result it is not useful to corroborate whom the claimant lived with and whether, he himself lived there. The claimant provided a second letter6 that stated that by 2004, the "XXXX family" was living in the particular house, "by the year 2004" however this date may refer to the claimant's sister and brother-in-law, or even brother who owned the house, but it does not corroborate that the claimant lived there, because the date mentioned is inconsistent with the date that the claimant alleged to have started living there, which was in 2005.7 Considering the two documents, the claimant's narrative and testimony, they are inconsistent and vague in what they are supposed to be confirming; the panel does not find them useful. This inconsistency, and vagueness, together with the claimant's testimony and narrative, raises a negative inference in the panel's mind as to the claimant's credibility.

When asked about the evening of the event with the FARC, "who was with you?" He answered "Sister, husband, and neighbor from the house next door." The panel further asked him, "Was your wife there?" he replied "No".

The claimant had said in the hearing room that he was living in the village for approximately 4 years, from 2005-2009, however the wife, only came for short periods, at limited periods, 3 to 4 times a year. He stated that sometimes he lived with himself and his wife, and sometimes with his brother and sister XXXX. The panel found the claimant's oral testimony inconsistent with the narrative. * His status as married.

The claimant explained that the marriage was a secret, because the claimant's first wife had died of a serious illness two years previously, and both he and his new wife had adult children, and they feared the shame and embarrassment of their respective families. While the idea that for an older man in his sixties, now aged 70, marrying a wife with similar contextual issues, may present challenges to the existing families, is plausible, there are inconsistencies in the claimant's behavior and in the testimony and narrative that lead the panel not to trust the credibility of the claimant.

There was no marriage certificate presented in the documents, and when asked about that, he said he didn't know he needed to present it and he could obtain it. The panel finds that this is an insufficient excuse considering the claimant was represented by extremely competent counsel, the claimant had been a Permanent Resident in the United States where he had lived for at least 6 years continuously so would have known the importance of documents for procedural matters, and applied for refugee protection since April 3, 2009. The panel draws a negative inference from the lack of documentation to support the "secret marriage" considering it is an important element in his claim. A "Secret Marriage."

Later on the panel asked the claimant why he had chosen to flee to his eldest sister's in Bogota, rather than go to his wife's home? He replied that the marriage was a secret that no one in the family knew. As the hearing progressed it appeared that some family members knew, and other did not, so it was unclear how much of a secret it really was, and the reasons.

The panel asked the claimant about his allegation of having lived in the house belonging to his brother in XXXX, with his sister and brother-in-law, as the panel was trying to get a picture of what happened, and where the wife would have been, realizing that often there are many details on the ground, that are explained in the hearing room. However there is at this point an inherent inconsistency between the narrative and the testimony. The claimant had stated in the narrative that he lived with his wife in this house during the period 2005-2009, and yet when questioned about her presence, he stated that she only lived there from time to time; that the only persons present at the time of the event in the house when the FARC arrived were himself, his sister, her husband and the neighbor. At this point the panel was not completely concerned, because it's possible that the wife had to turn her mind to her own family from time to time, given the age of the claimant.

As a result of the situation, the claimant quickly left XXXX, to hide out in Bogota; however the claimant never sought shelter at his wife's home, in XXXX, preferring his sister's in Bogota. The fact that the claimant chose to go to his sisters' rather than his wife's for fear of shame, is an indication of lack of subjective fear, as he would rather not be shamed. It seems to the panel on a balance of probabilities that a reasonable person would have sought help from a wife, whether a secret or not, in particular since the secrecy could provide added cover even though it would be embarrassing. As a result the panel draws a negative inference from this behavior. If the claimant is truly in fear of the FARC, and the marriage is a secret, then hiding out with his secret wife's family would provide a reasonable cover, which the claimant did not opt for.

The panel asked the claimant, "when you left the village, who were you with?" The claimant replied that he was with his sister and her husband. The panel then asked the claimant directly, where his wife was, and he replied that she was living with her aunt, also in semi-hiding because she herself was afraid. The panel asked, "if your marriage is a secret and you feared the FARC, why not go and live with her?" The reply, "Because her daughter is ill, and they don't know that we are married." From the other side of the family, the wife's side, it appears unreasonable that if the wife is in what was termed "semi-hiding" and if her daughter was seriously ill, that neither illness, fear of the FARC or the protection of a secret marriage would be a bar to hiding her husband from the FARC. The panel draws a negative inference from this. Permanent Residence in the USA.

The claimant with his first wife, had left Colombia in 1999 and had obtained Permanent Residence status in the USA, as a result of the sponsorship of his son. A second son, fled Colombia due to FARC persecution in 2001 and joined the family in the USA. A daughter came to Canada. Unfortunately, the claimant's first wife learned of having terminal cancer that year and unable to get medical care in the US, she returned to Colombia, with a third son, and remained in the care of her brother, until she passed away, a month later.
The claimant re-availed due to her passing, and then returned to the USA.

The claimant's son, who was the sponsoring relative, himself overcome by grief, and despair, suffered a severe mental depression. The claimant re-availed to Colombia a second time in XXXX 2003, with the purpose of re-marrying, and enabling the wife to return to the USA.

As his son had become disabled, and could not continue to support him, the claimant returned to Colombia, in 2005, and found a place to stay at the brother's home in XXXX, thus re-availing, and abandoning his US status. The claimant had permanent residence in the United States since 1999, due to the son's ability to support.

While it can be viewed as acceptable to return for a brief time to re-avail due to the death of his wife, the panel finds that returning for the purpose of marriage is quite another matter, in 2003. The claimant alleges that he had gotten married again in Colombia on XXXX, 2003.

At that point, this was a second time that he re-availed notwithstanding his fear of the FARC, as his desire to get married clearly overrode any fear he may have had. The claimant clearly chose to ignore any potential fear of FARC, because his wife's brother and nephew he alleged had been kidnapped as recently as XXXX in 2001.8
The claimant stated that he and his children had left Colombia, because of the FARC,9 however the claimant had never claimed asylum in the USA; as he had been sponsored.
The claimant had lived in the USA, sponsored by his son, with his first wife, who had become ill and died. He said his life in the USA was "hell".

The claimant abandoned his permanent residence in the USA. He was asked if he knew that leaving for a certain period of time would lead to abandonment of status and he said, yes. He was asked if he took any steps to maintain his status and he said, no. He was asked if it had occurred to him to maintain his US status and assist his son in his circumstances, and he responded that he did not have the capacity and the son had a wife and family. At the time he left the USA in 2005, he had turned his mind to staying in Colombia, and thus abandoned his status in the USA. The reason that he abandoned his status in the USA, was due to his marriage, which had taken priority over his fear. The panel concludes then, that he did not have a very strong fear of the FARC.
As a result, the claimant's abandonment of status in the USA indicates a lack of subjective fear.

The claimant relies on this particular incident, in XXXX for his claim, which contains inconsistencies in behavior and between the narrative and the testimony. As a result the panel does not trust the credibility of the claimant. Furthermore the claimant's behavior shows a lack of subjective fear, due to the reason which lead him to re-avail a second time to Colombia, and in abandoning the safety of his permanent residence which he had enjoyed for 6 years.
As a result the panel rejects the claim.
As a result I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee. Risk to his life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture

Due to the claimant's lack of credibility, and for the reasons above, I find that he is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to Colombia would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to cruel or unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

This claim is rejected.
